1. Data Overview

 
OVERVIEW OF THE DATASET:

https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/masoudnickparvar/brain-tumor-mri-dataset

In medical terms a simple way to explain a cancer is abnormal amount of cell growth in a particular region of a body part, in our case we have choosen a brain tumor dataset. As described early, Abrnormal growth of cells in the brain causes Brain Tumor/Cancer. This abnormal growth of the cells usually lead to seviere neurological damage in the brain. And main part is that early detection of the brain tumor is really critical for choosing an appropriate treatement.

Our Dataset consists of 4 categories:
* Giloma
* Meningioma
* Pituitary Tumor
* No tumor

we will now discuss about these:

GILOMA: Giloma is a tumor that grows in the regionof gilal cells- the supportive cells of the brain. This is the most common and dangerous of all 3.

MENINGIOMA: This is a tumor that grows from the meninges, the three layered membrance that wraps around the brain and spinal cord.

PITUITARY GLAND: The tumor which grows in the part of Pituitary gland in the brain is called as the pituitary tumor. Pituitary gland is a pea sized gland at the base of the brain that controls hormones.

NO TUMOR: As the name says these images show there is no tumor in the brain.

The dataset contain a total of 7200 images of brain MRI images and are divided into 4 categories. Giloma, Meningioma, Pituitary gland and No tumor.


The structure of the dataset is this:

1. Training:

Giloma - 1400 Images

Meningioma - 1400 Images

Pituitary gland - 1400 Images

No tumor - 1400 Images

2. Testing:

Giloma - 400 Images

Meningioma -400 Images

Pituitary - 400 Images

No tumor - 400 images

The dataset is derived from a source of 3 other datasets.

1. figshare brain MRI dataset - https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/brain_tumor_dataset/1512427

2. SARTAJ dataset - https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sartajbhuvaji/brain-tumor-classification-mri

3. Br35H dataset - https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ahmedhamada0/brain-tumor-detection?select=no

The images for the no tumor is gotten from the Br35H dataset.

According to the source, while the data was prepared they actually noticed some inconsistied in the giloma class of the SARTAJ dataset. To improve label reliability, these images were remoed and replaced.

There was also an important note that was mentioned in the source:

The size of the images may vary across the dataset and preprocessing steps are recommended before training the model.



What is the classification task?

The task for the model is to classify the image into any of the 4 categories that are mentioned, and it can be defined as single label image classification, and the reason. it looks like multi-tasking in reality it is assigning the image in one of the four is because the model is simultaneoulsy multiple different learning objectives. Classifying the tumor type and segmenting the tumor boundary.

SO IT IS A SINGLE LABEL IMAGE CLASSIFICATION

What business or policy case does it solve?

The world has a lot of people who carry the burden of brain cancer diagnosis. Manual classification of brain MRI scan requires a trained neuroradiologist, the proportianality for the amount and people and neuroradiologist are really less , and also the diagnostic process is time-intensive and subject to availability.

There is no buisness motive in building this model and in my opinion it should not be there. by building this model there are a lot of things that can be solved. for exapmle this will help us solve these below things.

1. Clinical decision support: Acts as an assistant for a meuroradiologist.
2. Helping automation: The model can prioritize which scans need immediate specialist attention.
3. Availabilty: In the regions of rurla hospitals which usually has limited neurology infrastructure, an AI-based classifier can help with early detection


Is this multi-task? Explain.

In general ML multi task learning is when a single model is trained to perform multiple task simultaneously, In Dl it refers to training a neural network to perform multiple task by sharing some common network parameters.

But what our model does is solving this question:

"WHich of these four categories does this scan come under- giloma, meningioma, pituitary tumor or no tumor?"

This is not a multi task problem. This is a single task problem becuase there is only one prediction objective(which is identify the tumor type). The model has only one output head. The dataset contains only one type of ground truth label per image.

To make this multi task the model would need to simultaneously produce multiple independent outputs with separate supervision. for example calculating malignancy score, this need malignancy labels(this is not in the dataset)

What is the feature data?

The feature data consists entirely of brain MRI 2d grayscale medical images of the human brain. each image is the raw pixel intensity array captured by an MRI scanner, where brighter regions indicate higher signal return from the tissue.

How it is stored?

The structure of the dataset is this:

1. Training:

Giloma - 1400 Images

Meningioma - 1400 Images

Pituitary gland - 1400 Images

No tumor - 1400 Images

2. Testing:

Giloma - 400 Images

Meningioma -400 Images

Pituitary - 400 Images

No tumor - 400 images

Who collected the data?

The dataset was compiled and published by Masoud Nickparvar in kaggle in teh year of 2021.

The dataset is derived from a source of 3 other datasets.

1. figshare brain MRI dataset - https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/brain_tumor_dataset/1512427

2. SARTAJ dataset - https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sartajbhuvaji/brain-tumor-classification-mri

3. Br35H dataset - https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ahmedhamada0/brain-tumor-detection?select=no

WHY? The data was collected to advance automated brain tumor detection and classification research.

When? In the year of 2021.

is the data multi-modal?

No the data is not multi-modal. the sole input is the 2D image of MRI scan of the brian Image. there is no other details of the pateint or anything else.

What evaluation criteria will you be using and why? Why does this support the business or policy case?

From the research that we have done this was the statement " A metric that looks good on paper can mask clinically dangerous failure modes". for this only we used a combination of 3 complemetary metrics: Macro-averaged F1- score, Per class precision, recall and Overall accuracy. each is chosen based on what it reveals about model behaviour in the context of brain tumor diagnosis.

F1 - it is the harmonic mean of Precision and recall for a given class. how this supports our buisness or policy case is because a patient with meningioma deserves the same diagnostic reliability as a patient with Glioma. macro F1 includes this clinical fairness at the metric level.\

Per class precision - precision and recall capture fundamentally different types of erro, and in the medical context these errors have deeply asymmetric real world impact.

overall accuracy - the fraction of all test image the model correctly classified. How this support the buisness policy it provides a clean number for comparng the model that we are using Simple CNN, Frozen swin, Fine- Tuned swin. and also it enables comparision against published literature on this dataset.

With the combination of above discussed metrtics our work will provide a complete diagnostic profile of each model.

2. Foundational Explanation


Foundational Model: Swin Transformer (Microsoft) | microsoft/swin-tiny-patch4-window7-224


2.1 Why Swin? The Evolution from CNNs and ViTs


Our team decided to use Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021), a model researched by the Microsoft team in Asia. This model has been researched by our team to determine which one is best suited for the data type of vision. Before explaining what the architecture of this model is, or what kind of data was already used to pretrain this model?

I want to go back to talk about two models that has been the good of a lot of deep learning model nowaday are: CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) and RNN ( Recurrent Neural Network). Those models are performing transformation by sequentials way, that lead to many problems if the data input is increase will cause to big O time complexity is O(n.d^2) and space complexity is O(n.d)[1]. Therefore, rather than still using RNN and CNN for many translation task or reading big documents, "Transformer" has been established and allow the to compute in a prallel way, lead to faster processing and bring great outcomes of translation [1].

In addition, Self-Attention is the core of many types of Transformers that make it better than RNN or CNN, as this mechanism allows Transformers to follow the global context by having long memory and faster computing (matrix multiplication) [1]. Besides, ViT also uses the Attention mechanism to look at the picture in a more global and intelligent way. It achieves this by evaluating the relationship of every part of the picture rather than just scanning small, localized areas as traditional solutions do [2]. However, even the model itself sounds good at handling vision processing, but one thing over here that is a naive way to apply Self-Attention to images would require each pixel to attend to every other pixel and lead to quadratic cost in the number of pixels O(n^2) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) [2]. Therefore, using Swin Transformer is our team's solution to avoid those shortcomings while doing this lab.

What tasks was the foundational model trained upon?

Our foundational model is Swin-Tiny (Shifted Window Transformer), specifically the microsoft/swin-tiny-patch4-window7-224 published by Microsoft research. Understanding what it was trained on is essential to understanding why transfer learning works so well for our brain tumor task. Swin-Tiny was primarily trained on ImageNet, a large scall image classification benchmark. Around 1.28 million training images. 1000 object classes

2.2 Achitectural of Swin Transformer & How its Process:


Swin methodology is using Attention mechnism and CNN design to make the architecture to be a Hierarchical Feature Maps like CNN, as it progresses through deeper layer, it merge groups of pixels together, which in the architecture is called Patch Merging [3]. For more details, we can look at the picture of Swin Architecture below:

Check below image

The architecture of Swin is a hirarchical process to show how picture go through a total of four distinct stages. Inititally, pictures go through a patch partition to divide the input into 4x4 patches since this is swin tiny patch and flatten each patch to a 48-dimensional vector (4 x 4 x 3 = 48 (3 is RGB color) [3]. From this, it can be observed that as one proceeds deeper into the layers, the resolution is halved at each successive stage (H/4 -> H/8 -> H/16 -> H/32), as you can see the model is zooming out to seeing the whole picture. Furthermore, on the right side, architecture B illustrates the micro-design inside the Swin Transformer Block. In the first block, W-MSA, this is the step of divide and conquer (recursion), as the picture below showing that how patches separate and communicate 4 windows, the attention mechanism allow patches to communciate with other patches that locate in the same window. Then, SW-MSA shifts the window slightly downward and to the right by a distance equal to half the window size. Based on this mechanism, information from one window is spreaded over to the other one and keeps doing it until every infomrmation is propagated throughout the entire image.

Check image below

* Storagre of Swin model: 28M Parameters
* Linear Complexity: O(n)

2.3 Pre-training Tasks and Objectives


2.3.1 Pre-training Tasks:


Main task: Image Classification is used for the pre-training phase.
Data Using for Pre-Train:
- Imagenet-1k is the main data for the pre-training phase, which contains 1.28 millions picture that for training, 50,000 for validation, and 100,000 for testing [4].
- 1000 different object categories such as dog, cat, transportation, etc [4].

2.3.2 Training Objectives of Model:


Previous Training Objectives:
- Hierarchical Feature Maps: Compared to traditional ViT, which only supports a single scale and is fit for image classification [2]. Swin Transformer is built on an architecture that is hierarchical as CNN, which utilizing shifted window mechanism to transform information of each window, enabling the model to capture high-level, intricate details of the image.
- Optimize Computing Cost: ViT traditional is cost quadratic in the number of pixels, which leads to time and space complexity of O (n^2). Swin Transformer using the new two mechanisms, W-MSA and SW-MSA, makes the model more scalable and able to handle high pixel pictures that traditional models can not handle.

New Training Objectives:
- Because this model excels at capturing details in images, our team decided to utilize a Brain Tumor MRI dataset. Our goal is to train the model to identify the subtle characteristics of four different types of brain tumors. Ultimately, this will assist doctors in diagnosing tumors with even higher accuracy.

2.4 Domain Analysis:


- This is a cross-domain task. Based on our research regarding this model, our team decided to implement a new training task focused on a completely different domain: HealthCare.
- Our new task will use data from Medical Imaging (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/masoudnickparvar/brain-tumor-mri-dataset)
- Despite differences in domain, the fundamental characteristics of the brain or the structure of tumors still quite similarities to natural imagery; for instance, the surface of a lake can be same a tumorous mass. With this approach to transfer learning, the model does not need to learn from 0.

A: Data Splitting

There are already two folders in this dataset; Training and Testing. The classes are classified into four subfolders in each folder; glioma, meningioma, notumor and pituitary.

We did not divide the data by ourselves. The author separated the images of 3 sources of the population into 5600 training images and 1600 testing images (77.8/22.2). This ratio is acceptable since the training set is large enough to be trained and the test set is large enough to determine the performance.

Stratification:
The following code demonstretes the number of pictures in training and testing of each class. We would like to have the simillarity of class proportions in both sets. An example of this is when we have 25 experiments with glioma as training images, we would also find that 25 percent of test images would also be glioma. Provided that the proportions were quite different, we might have conducted a false evaluation.

It is not a multi-task dilemma. The task is as follows: find what categories of MRI images correspond to the following four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor and no tumor.

Why this split is reasonable:
- The model has been tested on images that it has never seen in training, hence, performance can be trusted.
- Before the processing of the data, we split the image level and therefore we do not leak data.
- The ratio of classes is approximately equal between training and testing and hence the test scores are indicative of performance in the real world.

A: Loss Function

PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss, which is the common loss of multi-class classification, is used by us.

The reason why CrossEntropyLoss is the right choice in this case:
- There are 4 exclusive classes. This is the reason why CrossEntropyLoss is used.
- It uses the raw outputs and applies LogSoftmax to them and calculates the negative log likelihood, indicating how similar the predicted probabilities are to the true labels.
- It puts a heavy penalty on confident wrong predictions and a heavy reward on confident right predictions and results in well-calibrated probabilities.
- operating on integer labels (0, 1, 2, 3), identical to ImageFolder labels used by pytorch.


We use only this loss. There are no other losses required since there is just one classification task and one output head. We are not performing segmentation, detection, and other activities, which require additional losses.

import os
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from collections import Counter

# Paths (update if your folder structure is different)
TRAIN_DIR = "/content/archive/Training"
TEST_DIR  = "/content/archive/Testing"

# Load datasets just to inspect structure
temp_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
])

train_dataset = datasets.ImageFolder(root=TRAIN_DIR, transform=temp_transform)
test_dataset  = datasets.ImageFolder(root=TEST_DIR,  transform=temp_transform)

class_names = train_dataset.classes
train_labels = [label for _, label in train_dataset.samples]
test_labels  = [label for _, label in test_dataset.samples]

train_counts = Counter(train_labels)
test_counts  = Counter(test_labels)

# Print distribution

print("DATASET SPLIT SUMMARY:")

print(f"Total images:    {len(train_dataset) + len(test_dataset)}")
print(f"Training images: {len(train_dataset)} ({100*len(train_dataset)/(len(train_dataset)+len(test_dataset)):.1f}%)")
print(f"Testing images:  {len(test_dataset)} ({100*len(test_dataset)/(len(train_dataset)+len(test_dataset)):.1f}%)")

print(f"\n{'Class':<15} {'Train':>8} {'Train %':>10} {'Test':>8} {'Test %':>10}")
print("-" * 55)
for i, name in enumerate(class_names):
    tr = train_counts[i]
    te = test_counts[i]
    tr_pct = 100 * tr / len(train_dataset)
    te_pct = 100 * te / len(test_dataset)
    print(f"{name:<15} {tr:>8} {tr_pct:>9.1f}% {te:>8} {te_pct:>9.1f}%")

From the above figs, we can see:

1. The author has already split the data into training and test data, with 77.8% for training and 22.2% for the test data.
2. All classes have almost the same percentage in the training and test data. None of the classes is more or less represented in data.
3. There is small variation in the representation of each type of tumor. Glioma and meningioma have more data than pituitary and no tumor. However, this variation is similar in the training and test data, and thus it is fair.
4. We used only one CrossEntropyLosss function. This is the standard and the best way to do it when we have four classes and each image is represented by exactly one class.

# TASK 4 — BASELINE: Simple 3-Layer CNN (From Scratch)



import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import torch.optim as optim

#Model Definition
class SimpleCNN(nn.Module):
    """
    A minimal 3-block CNN baseline.
    Deliberately simple to contrast with the Swin Transformer:
      - No attention mechanism
      - No patch embeddings
      - No skip/residual connections
      - No pretrained weights
      - Global Average Pooling instead of large FC layers
        keeps parameter count low (~94K total)
    """
    def __init__(self, num_classes=4):
        super(SimpleCNN, self).__init__()

        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            # Block 1
            # Input: (B, 3, 224, 224)
            nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),   # → (B, 32, 224, 224)
            nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),         # → (B, 32, 112, 112)

            # Block 2
            nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),  # → (B, 64, 112, 112)
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),         # → (B, 64, 56, 56)

            # Block 3
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1), # → (B, 128, 56, 56)
            nn.BatchNorm2d(128),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),

            # Global Average Pooling — collapses spatial dims
            # → (B, 128, 1, 1)  — avoids giant FC layer
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)),
        )

        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),               # → (B, 128)
            nn.Dropout(p=0.5),
            nn.Linear(128, num_classes) # → (B, 4)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        x = self.classifier(x)
        return x


# Hyperparameters
TASK4_EPOCHS     = 20
TASK4_BATCH_SIZE = 32
TASK4_LR         = 1e-3

# DataLoaders
task4_train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset,
    batch_size=TASK4_BATCH_SIZE,
    shuffle=True,
    num_workers=2,
    pin_memory=True
)
task4_test_loader = DataLoader(
    test_dataset,
    batch_size=TASK4_BATCH_SIZE,
    shuffle=False,
    num_workers=2,
    pin_memory=True
)

# Build Model
task4_model = SimpleCNN(num_classes=NUM_CLASSES).to(DEVICE)

task4_total_params     = sum(p.numel() for p in task4_model.parameters())
task4_trainable_params = sum(p.numel() for p in task4_model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)


print("Baseline Model: Simple 3-Layer CNN (From Scratch)")
print(f"  Total parameters:     {task4_total_params:,}")
print(f"  Trainable parameters: {task4_trainable_params:,}")
print(f"  Approx model size:    {task4_total_params * 4 / (1024**2):.4f} MB")
print(f"\n  Compare to Swin-Tiny: ~28,000,000 parameters")
print(f"  SimpleCNN is {28_000_000 // task4_total_params}x smaller than Swin-Tiny\n")
print(task4_model)

# Loss, Optimizer, Scheduler

task4_optimizer = optim.Adam(
    task4_model.parameters(),

# StepLR: reduce LR by 10x every 7 epochs

# Training

We have utilizing simple 3 layer CNN, which we trained from scratch, all the weights are random, and learned from the brain tumor MRI images.

This is a baseline model which is simple architecturally and distinct from the swin trasformer .

the model consists of three convolutional block and avg pooling and sinlge linear classifier:

Block 1: Conv(3-32) + BatchNorm + ReLU + MaxPool → 112×112

Block 2: Conv(32-64) + BatchNorm + ReLU + MaxPool → 56×56

Block 3: Conv(64-128) + BatchNorm + ReLU + GlobalAvgPool → 1×1

Classifier: Flatten → Dropout(0.5) → Linear(128→4)

global avg pool replaces large fully connected layers, and also keeping the parameters count around 94k, which is. much smaller than swin-tiny's 28M parameters

def train_one_epoch_finetuned(model, loader, criterion, optimizer, device):
    model.train()
    running_loss = 0.0
    correct = 0
    total = 0
    for images, labels in loader:
        images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(images)
        logits = outputs.logits
        loss = criterion(logits, labels)
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        optimizer.step()
        running_loss += loss.item() * images.size(0)
        _, predicted = logits.max(1)
        total += labels.size(0)
        correct += predicted.eq(labels).sum().item()
    return running_loss / total, correct / total

We now unfreeze the last two Swin stages (Stages 2 and 3), LayerNorm, classification head, while keeping the early layers (embeddings and Stages 0 and 1) frozen. This will adjust the high-level features according to brain MRI patterns while keeping low-level features constant.


Key techniques to ensure convergence:
1. Differential learning rates: backbone = 1e-5,and also head = 1e-3. This helps prevent catastrophic forgetting.
2. Gradient clipping with max_norm = 1.0. This is used to prevent gradients from exploding.
3. AdamW with weight decay = 0.01 on the backbone. This ensures the weights are not pushed away from their pre-trained values.
4. Cosine annealing learning rate schedule. This is used for a smooth learning rate decrease.
5. Batch size 16 instead of 32. This is used to reduce memory usage on the GPU since we have many parameters with gradients.

result: The highest accuracy among the three models.

import numpy as np

print("Re-evaluating all three models on the test set...\n")

def get_predictions(model, loader, device, is_huggingface=False):
    model.eval()
    all_preds, all_labels = [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, labels in loader:
            images = images.to(device)
            if is_huggingface:
                logits = model(images).logits
            else:
                logits = model(images)
            preds = logits.argmax(dim=1).cpu().numpy()
            all_preds.extend(preds)
            all_labels.extend(labels.numpy())
    return np.array(all_labels), np.array(all_preds)

Now I will discuss the results and discussion.

In general we trained and evaluted three models on the brain tumor MRI dataset to classify images into 4 categories which are Giloma, Meningioma, Pituitary tumor and No tumor. The 3 models represent a progression from a simple baseline trained from scartch, to transfer learning with frozen backbone, to full fine tuning of the foundational swin-tiny tranformer.

Model 1 - Simple CNN (From scratch)

Setup - The baseline model is a 3 layer CNN with around 94k trainable parameters. it uses 3 convolutional blocks(conv - batchNorm - ReLU - pooling). followed by global average pooling and a single linear classification head. all the weights are randomly initialized- no pretrained knowledge is used, and also the model was trained on 20 epochs using Adam and with learing rate of 1e-3 with a batch size of 32.

The simple CNN got around a 75% overall accuracy, which is well above the 25% random baseline for a 4-class problem.

Convergence: The training loss decreased stedily across all the 20 epochs, confirming the model converged. the test accuracy started going in a single line
around epoch 12-15, indicating the model reached its max performance. The gap between training and test accuracy suggests mild overfitting expected given the model must learn all visual features from only 5,600 images with no prior knowledge.

We think that 75% accuracy establishes the lower bound for the task. The models capacity which is 94K means that it can detect broad discriminative pattern in the MRI scans but struggles with the very small visual difference between the tumor types

Model 2 - Swin-Tiny(frozen backbone).

We loaded the swin-tiny model pretrained on the imagenet and replaced its 1k class head with a new linear(768-4) head for our tumor classes . the entire swin backbone(28.3 M parameters) was frozen - only the 3067 classification head parameters were trained. the model was trained on 15 epochs using Adam (lr = 1e-3) with pre trained features with no adaptation of the backbone to MRI data.

Convergence: The model actually converged rapidly and the test accuracy stabilized by epoch 5 and remained same till reaching 10 epochs. this is actually quite expected because with only 3076 parameters training, the optimization is small.

the 10% improvement over the baseline demonstrated the power of transfer learning - the ImageNet features generalize effectively to MRI scans despite being learned on the natural images. But from the 85% ceiling gives us a limitation: the frozen backbone cannot adapt to the MRI- specific patterns, this might not be good for subtle tumor charactersitcs in medical scans.

Model 3 - Swin-Tiny(Fine tuned)

In this we completely used Swin-Tiny weights but this time we used the complete model with all the 28.3M parameters.

we used graident cliiping for stable training and AdamW optimizer with weight decay = 0.01 in. backbone. The batch size is reduced to 16 to accommodate larger gradient memory from the unfrozen layers.

Convergence: The model actually converged really smoothly ov er 15 epochs. the results were stable decreasing the loss curves without the sudden drops. The train and test gap was much smaller than the previous two models, indicating the better generalization. the adapted backbone provides representations tuned to MRI data rather than generic ImageNet features.

The 95% accuracy demonstrates the fine tuning is the most effective startegy for this dataset. by allowing the high level swin stages to adapt to brain MRI patterns while preserving low level general features.

Also discuss and compare the convergence of the models as well as the run time and memory needed.

CONVERGENCE COMPARISION

Simple CNN - Epoch-15 -- train/test gap- 15%

Swin Forzen - Epoch-5 -- train/test gap - ~6%

Swin Fine-Tuned - Epoch-10 -- train/test gap ~ 3%

From the convergence plots clearly show the three different behaviours. the simple CNN converges slowly and shows the largest overfitting gap. the frozen swin coverges fast but reaches flat line smoothly with the smallest train/test gap and highest final accuracy.

Run time required

Simple CNN - 6.8 min
Swin Twin frozen - 5 min
Swin Twin fine tuned model - 5.1 min

Memory Analysis

Simple CNN - very low(0.4 mb)
Swin Frozen - Low (108 mb)
Swin fine tuned - High(~108mb)

Does Fine-Tuning support the policy Case?

Yes strongly. a 95% accurate automated brain tumor classifier trained on just 5,600 images shows that:

Clinical clarity: close radiologist accuracy is achievable without massive proprietary clinical datasets,making deployment feasible in under resourced hospitals as we discussed in the top section.

Cost efficiency: Fine-tuning a pretrained model requires significantly less compute than training from scratch the majority of learning came free from ImageNet pretraining.

Per-class reliability: The fine-tuned model achieves high recall across all four classes, including the clinically critical Glioma class where missed detections are most dangerous.

Advantages of Fine-Tuning

Highest accuracy and macro F1 of all three approaches, Smallest train/test gap best generalization ,pretrained knowledge adapting to MRI
effective even with a small dataset (5,600 images), per-class recall is consistently high across all classes

Limitations

Requires GPU: fine-tuning 14M parameters is not feasible on CPU limits deployment in low-resource settings without inference optimization.

2D images only: The dataset provides single 2D slices.
Real clinical diagnosis uses 3D volumetric MRI sequences

No patient metadata: Age, symptoms, and clinical
history are all ignored. Real radiologists use this
context the model operates without it.

Balanced dataset: The perfectly balanced 25%/class
split may not be in the realworld prevalence where no
Tumor cases are far more common performance in
deployment could differ from test set results.

Single 2D slice per patient: A real MRI scan has
hundreds of slices. Our model sees one — it could miss
tumors that appear on other slices.
